newsitem.title: FRANCE: France trims intervention rate to 3.25 pct.
newsitem.headline: France trims intervention rate to 3.25 pct.

text.p: The Bank of France trimmed a key interest rate Thursday in an apparent sign of its approval of the conservative government's 1997 budget.
The Bank said it was lowering its intervention rate to 3.25 percent from 3.35 percent at a money market tender.
The Bank left the five-to-10 day rate, which is considered less important at the moment, unchanged at 4.75 percent.
"It is a validation of the budget," Credit Lyonnais economist Valerie Asselot said.
"It means the Bank of France did not see the budget as being a threat in terms of inflation or the franc," Societe Generale economist Michala Marcussen added.

On Wednesday the government unveiled a 1997 budget that lowered spending in real terms and allowed France to meet Maastricht treaty criteria on European monetary union. But the government had to resort to exceptional revenues, such as a payment from France Telecom to cover pension liabilities in the years ahead, to meet its goal.

Economists had been split on whether the Bank would cut interest rates on Thursday, with some saying they expected it to wait for the dust to settle after the budget, especially given a slight weakening in the franc against the mark.
The franc was trading at 3.4063 per mark shortly after the rate cut, lower than before the budget announcement but off the low of 3.4092 it reached on Wednesday.

In cutting the intervention rate, the Bank of France narrowed the premium of French official rates over German rates which had widened after the Bundesbank cut its repo rate to 3.00 percent from 3.30 percent on August 22.
Economists said the Bank of France still had room to trim the intervention rate further, though only by a small amount.
"By only catching up with the Bundesbank they've signalled they're being cautious. They could have done more and been OK," said Sonja Gibbs, at Nomura International.
